title: R Analysis on Cumulative Confirmed Cases of COVID-19 in BC
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

Data: COVID-19 Data Repository by the Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University, licensed CC BY 4.0, © Johns Hopkins University 2020.

Dong E, Du H, Gardner L. An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real time. Lancet Infect Dis. 2020;20(5):533-534. doi: 10.1016/S1473-3099(20)30120-1

This R code is adapted from DSCI523: Programming for Data Manipulation (Lab 2)
In this analysis, I will be analyzing the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases between June 2021 and September 2021 in R. This analysis is the same analysis I did in my other blog post with Python.

url <- "https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19/raw/master/csse_covid_19_data/csse_covid_19_time_series/time_series_covid19_confirmed_global.csv"
covid_global <- read_csv(url)

three_months <- interval(start = ymd("2021-06-10"), end = ymd("2021-09-10"))

First, I read in the CSV file from the URL and extracted the 3 month interval between June 2021 and September 2021 using the interval() function from the “lubridate” package in R. Since both dates were in the format ‘%y-%m-$d’, I used the ymd() function to convert these to date objects.

bc_covid19_confirmed_3_months <- covid_global |>
  filter(`Province/State` == "British Columbia")  |>
  select(5:ncol(covid_global)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "date",
               values_to = "confirmed_cases") |>
  mutate(date = mdy(date)) |>
  filter(date %within% three_months)

bc_covid19_confirmed_3_months

# A tibble: 93 × 2
   date       confirmed_cases
   <date>               <dbl>
 1 2021-06-10          145996
 2 2021-06-11          146176
 3 2021-06-12          146176
 4 2021-06-13          146176
 5 2021-06-14          146453
 6 2021-06-15          146561
 7 2021-06-16          146674
 8 2021-06-17          146794
 9 2021-06-18          146902
10 2021-06-19          146902
# ℹ 83 more rows


This code chunk was taken directly from the lab2 assignment (as it was provided starter code). Here, a pipeline is created that filters relevant rows, selects columns we are interested in, performs the pivot to reshape the dataframe into a long format, adds a new date column, and finally filters the data so that we only consider dates within the three month interval. From the tibble that is outputted, we have an exact count of the number of confirmed cases for every month in our 3 month interval.

ggplot(bc_covid19_confirmed_3_months, aes(x = date, y = confirmed_cases)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Cumulative confirmed cases") +
  theme_bw()







Figure 1: Cumulative confirmed COVID-19 cases in BC, June–September 2021.





From this plot, notice that there is an upward trend in the number of confirmed cases from June 2021 to September 2021. This observation aligns with my results from the Python analysis as similar trends were present.

title: Python Analysis on Cumulative Confirmed Cases of COVID-19 in BC
text:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Data: COVID-19 Data Repository by the Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University, licensed CC BY 4.0, © Johns Hopkins University 2020.

Dong E, Du H, Gardner L. An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real time. Lancet Infect Dis. 2020;20(5):533-534. doi: 10.1016/S1473-3099(20)30120-1

This python code is adapted from DSCI523: Programming for Data Manipulation (Lab 2)
In this analysis, I will be analyzing the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases between June 2021 and September 2021. During these 3 months, the COVID-19 pandemic was quite relevant across media and impacted social gatherings, meetups, and education alike.

url = "https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19/raw/master/csse_covid_19_data/csse_covid_19_time_series/time_series_covid19_confirmed_global.csv"
covid_global = pd.read_csv(url)

bc_rows = covid_global[covid_global["Province/State"] == "British Columbia"]
date_cols = covid_global.columns[4:]

First, I read in the data from the URL and filtered for only the rows in the dataset where the value of “Province/State” was “British Columbia”. I indexed only the date columns in the dataset by indexing from column 4 to the last column (as these were all dates).

bc_long = bc_rows.melt(id_vars=["Province/State"], value_vars=date_cols,
                       var_name="date", value_name="confirmed_cases")
bc_long["date"] = pd.to_datetime(bc_long["date"], format="%m/%d/%y")

bc_covid = bc_long[(bc_long["date"] >= "2021-06-10") & (bc_long["date"] <= "2021-09-10")].copy()

I then melted the original dataframe into a long format so that there is a new column called ‘date’ with all the date values and a new column called confirmed_cases with values for the number of confirmed cases for each date. Since the date column is not inherently a datetime variable, I needed to explicitly convert the variable into datetime using Pandas with the correct format. Lastly, in this step, I filtered for only the dates between 2021/06/10 and 2021/09/10 to look at how the number of cumulative cases changed over these 3 months.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(bc_covid["date"], bc_covid["confirmed_cases"], color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative confirmed cases")
plt.xticks(rotation=25, ha="right")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Cumulative confirmed COVID-19 cases in BC, June–September 2021.





From this plot, notice that there is clearly an increasing trend for the number of cumulative cases in BC as we went through the Summer of 2021. In particular, cases started to rise substantially starting in August and throughout September.
